question: What is the current statutory name and citation for Pennsylvania's seller property-condition disclosure statute?
choice_a: The Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7301-7315
choice_b: The Property Condition Disclosure Act, 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 1-50
choice_c: The Homeowner Protection Act, 35 P.S. Sections 750-799
explanation: The Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law is codified at 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7301-7315, part of the broader Residential Real Estate Transfers Law (68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7101-7512), which also includes the separate Home Inspection Law at Sections 7501-7513.
source_note: 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7301-7315 (confirmed verbatim via the official pa.gov Seller Disclosure Law PDF, extracted via pdftotext)

question: What must a Pennsylvania seller disclose to a buyer under Section 7303 of the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law?
choice_a: Only defects the seller has personally repaired within the last year
choice_b: Any material defects with the property known to the seller, by completing all applicable items on a property disclosure statement
choice_c: Only defects a licensed home inspector has already identified
choice_d: Nothing -- the law only requires disclosure to a lender, not the buyer
explanation: Section 7303 requires any seller who intends to transfer real property to disclose to the buyer any material defects known to the seller, by completing all applicable items in a property disclosure statement meeting Section 7304's requirements.

question: By when must the signed, dated property disclosure statement be delivered to the buyer under Section 7303?
choice_b: At any point before the deed is recorded
choice_c: Prior to the signing of an agreement of transfer by the seller and buyer
choice_d: There is no delivery deadline under the statute
explanation: Section 7303 requires the signed, dated disclosure statement to be delivered to the buyer, per the delivery methods in Section 7305, PRIOR to the seller and buyer signing an agreement of transfer -- ensuring the buyer has the information before becoming contractually bound.

question: Which of the following residential transfers is EXEMPT from the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law under Section 7302?
choice_a: Any resale of a home more than 10 years old
choice_b: Any transfer where the sale price exceeds $500,000
choice_c: Any transfer handled by a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: New residential construction not previously occupied, where the buyer receives a 1-year-or-longer written warranty, the dwelling passed a code-compliance inspection, and a certificate of occupancy/code compliance was issued
explanation: Section 7302(A)(2) exempts new, previously-unoccupied residential construction from the disclosure chapter, but only when all three conditions are met: a written warranty of at least 1 year, a code-compliance inspection, and issuance of a certificate of occupancy or code compliance.

question: Which of these transfers is excluded from the entire Residential Real Estate Transfers Law (both the definitional 'residential real estate transfer' scope AND the disclosure chapter) under Section 7101's exceptions?
choice_a: Transfers pursuant to court order, including probate, writ of execution, bankruptcy trustee, eminent domain, and specific-performance decrees
choice_b: Any sale to a first-time homebuyer
choice_c: Any transfer of a condominium unit, regardless of common-element status
choice_d: Any transfer where the buyer waives disclosure in the agreement of sale
explanation: The Section 7101 definitional exceptions carve out court-ordered transfers (probate administration, writs of execution, bankruptcy trustee transfers, eminent domain/condemnation, and specific-performance decrees), foreclosure-related transfers, transfers between co-owners or to a spouse/lineal relative, corporate liquidation distributions, transfers for non-residential conversion/demolition, and transfers of unimproved real property.
source_note: 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7101(B) exceptions (confirmed verbatim via the official pa.gov Seller Disclosure Law PDF)

question: Is a foreclosure-related transfer (e.g., a mortgagee acquiring property via foreclosure sale or a deed in lieu of foreclosure) subject to the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law?
choice_a: Yes -- foreclosure sales are fully subject to the same disclosure obligations as an ordinary resale
choice_b: No -- foreclosure-related transfers, including deeds in lieu of foreclosure, are excluded
choice_c: Only judicial foreclosures are excluded; non-judicial transfers are not
choice_d: The exclusion applies only if the mortgagee is a bank, not an individual lender
explanation: Section 7101(B)(2) excludes transfers to a mortgagee by a defaulting mortgagor, foreclosure sales after default, and transfers via deed in lieu of foreclosure from the disclosure law's scope -- reflecting that these are distressed, lender-driven transfers rather than voluntary owner-to-buyer sales.

question: For a condominium unit sale, how far does a Pennsylvania seller's disclosure obligation under the Seller Disclosure Law extend?
choice_a: To the entire condominium building, including every other owner's unit
choice_b: The Seller Disclosure Law does not apply to condominiums at all, under any circumstance
choice_c: Only to the seller's own unit -- disclosures about common elements or common facilities are governed separately (by the resales-of-units provision)
choice_d: Only to units sold for cash, not those financed by a mortgage
explanation: Section 7302(B) limits a condo unit seller's Seller Disclosure Law obligation to the seller's own unit; disclosures concerning common elements or common facilities are instead governed by the resales-of-units provision (Section 3407) and, for cooperatives, Section 4409.

question: If the seller does not know or cannot obtain an item of required disclosure information, what may the seller do under Section 7306?
choice_a: Leave that item entirely blank with no further obligation
choice_b: Refuse to sell the property until the information is obtained
choice_c: Delegate the entire disclosure form to the buyer's own inspector
choice_d: Make the disclosure based on the best information available to the seller
explanation: Section 7306 allows a seller, when an item of required information is unknown or unavailable at disclosure time, to make the disclosure based on the best information reasonably available -- the law does not require the seller to conduct new investigations to fill every gap.

question: Is a Pennsylvania seller required by the Seller Disclosure Law to conduct an independent investigation to complete the property disclosure statement?
choice_a: No -- Section 7308 states the seller has no affirmative duty to investigate, but must not knowingly make false, deceptive, or misleading statements, and must not fail to disclose a known material defect
choice_b: Yes -- sellers must hire a licensed inspector before completing the form
choice_c: Yes -- sellers must obtain a certified appraisal before completing the form
choice_d: No investigation duty exists, and there is no penalty for knowingly omitting a known defect
explanation: Section 7308 draws a careful line: no affirmative investigation duty exists, but the seller may not knowingly (or with reason to know) make false, deceptive, or misleading representations, and may not fail to disclose a KNOWN material defect -- the standard is actual/constructive knowledge, not an obligation to go looking for problems.

question: Under Section 7309, when is a seller NOT liable for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in the required disclosures?
choice_a: A seller is strictly liable for every disclosure error regardless of knowledge or reliance on experts
choice_b: When the seller had no knowledge of it, reasonably believed a defect had been corrected, or relied on information from a public agency, home inspector, contractor, or licensed professional acting within their expertise
choice_c: Only if the buyer signed a liability waiver at closing
choice_d: Sellers are never liable for disclosure errors under any circumstance, even with actual knowledge
explanation: Section 7309(A) provides three specific safe harbors: no knowledge of the error, a reasonable belief the defect had already been corrected, or reliance on information from a public agency or a qualified home inspector/contractor/licensed professional acting within the scope of their expertise, when the seller lacked knowledge of the error.

question: Under Section 7310, when may an AGENT (as opposed to the seller) be held liable for a violation of the Seller Disclosure Law?
choice_a: An agent is automatically liable for any disclosure defect regardless of the agent's own knowledge
choice_b: Agents are entirely immune from liability under the Seller Disclosure Law, even with actual knowledge of fraud
choice_c: Only if the agent had actual knowledge of a material defect that was not disclosed to the buyer, or of a misrepresentation relating to a material defect
choice_d: Only if the agent personally drafted the disclosure form
explanation: Section 7310 sets a narrower liability standard for agents than for sellers: an agent of the seller or buyer is not liable under the chapter unless the agent had ACTUAL knowledge of an undisclosed material defect or of a misrepresentation relating to one.

question: If a seller fails entirely to comply with the Seller Disclosure Law, is the resulting real estate transfer automatically invalidated?
choice_a: Yes -- any noncompliance automatically voids the entire transaction
choice_b: No -- and there is no damages remedy of any kind for noncompliance
choice_c: The transfer is only invalidated if the buyer sues within 10 days of closing
choice_d: No -- Section 7311(A) states a transfer is not invalidated solely for noncompliance, but a willful or negligent violator is liable for the buyer's actual damages
explanation: Section 7311(A) protects the finality of closed transactions: noncompliance alone does not unwind the transfer, but a person who willfully or negligently violates the disclosure chapter remains liable for the buyer's actual damages, without limiting a court's separate authority to award punitive damages or apply other remedies under other law.

question: Under the national broker content outline, which federal environmental statute is associated with the acronym CERCLA, tested alongside property condition and environmental disclosures?
choice_a: The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (the federal 'Superfund' law)
choice_b: The Clean Rivers and Coastal Land Act
choice_c: The Community Environmental Reinvestment and Compliance Loan Act
choice_d: A Pennsylvania-only statute with no federal counterpart
explanation: CERCLA, tested under the national outline's Section VI.A.3.a, is the federal 'Superfund' law addressing hazardous-substance cleanup liability, further amended by the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA) referenced in the same subtopic.
source_note: Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, effective April 1, 2025, Section VI.A.3.a-b (confirmed directly from the official candidate handbook PDF)

question: Does Pennsylvania legally require a seller to test a home for radon before listing it for sale?
choice_a: Yes -- every home sold in Pennsylvania must have a current radon test
choice_b: No -- Pennsylvania does not mandate radon testing, but once a test HAS been performed, the results must be disclosed as a known material defect if elevated
choice_c: No -- and even known elevated test results never need to be disclosed
choice_d: Only commercial properties are ever required to test for radon
explanation: Pennsylvania does not compel pre-listing radon testing, so a seller who never tested has no results to disclose; but once a test has been conducted, the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law's material-defect disclosure obligation (Section 7304(B)(14), 'Presence of hazardous substances') requires known elevated radon results to be disclosed and cannot be withheld.
source_note: 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7304(B)(14) (confirmed verbatim, cross-referenced from earlier in this bucket); radon testing NOT being mandatory confirmed via research pass citing PA Radon Certification Act materials and parealtors.org guidance

question: Which Pennsylvania statute certifies and regulates individuals and businesses that perform radon testing and mitigation services?
choice_a: The Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law itself directly certifies radon professionals
choice_c: The Radon Certification Act, 63 P.S. Sections 2001-2014
choice_d: There is no state certification requirement for radon professionals in Pennsylvania
explanation: The Radon Certification Act, 63 P.S. Sections 2001-2014, implemented through 25 Pa. Code Chapter 240, requires individuals and businesses performing radon testing, mitigation, and related services in Pennsylvania to be state-certified -- a separate regulatory scheme from the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law's substantive disclosure obligations.
source_note: 63 P.S. Sections 2001-2014; 25 Pa. Code Chapter 240 (confirmed via research pass citing PA DEP's Bureau of Radiation Protection materials)

question: If information disclosed under the Seller Disclosure Law is later rendered inaccurate before final settlement due to a subsequent event, what must the seller do under Section 7307?
choice_a: Nothing -- the original disclosure remains binding regardless of later developments
choice_b: Cancel the agreement of sale automatically
choice_c: Wait until closing day to mention any changes
choice_d: Notify the buyer of the inaccuracy
explanation: Section 7307 imposes an ongoing duty: if a disclosed item becomes inaccurate before final settlement because of some act, occurrence, or agreement after the disclosures were delivered, the seller must notify the buyer of that inaccuracy -- the disclosure obligation does not end the moment the form is signed.
